From Insight to Authorship

From Insight to Authorship

18 Aug

From Insight to Authorship

By Dr Ben Koh, MCC
Founder, Coach Masters Academy | Two-time Thinkers50 Coaches50 honouree

To be recognised for a second time in Thinkers50’s Coaches50 is a meaningful honour. I receive it not as a conclusion to the work, but as a responsibility to continue examining what professional coaching must next become capable of enabling. The question that continues to shape my work is not how coaching can do more of the same, but how the profession can deepen its understanding of human change.

Professional coaching has advanced considerably in its capacity to create reflection, surface insight, and support purposeful action. Yet a more difficult question remains.

What happens when a person understands what must change, but finds that the same response returns when authority, relationship, uncertainty or risk enters the situation?

This article argues that the next frontier of professional coaching begins at the point of action.

When Insight Is Not Yet Change

Coaching is often valued for the insight it generates. It can bring previously unrecognised patterns into awareness, challenge assumptions that have shaped a leader’s choices, and reframe situations that once seemed fixed.

Insight, however, is not self-executing. A leader may understand a pattern with exceptional clarity and still reproduce it when under pressure, and consequences reassert themselves.

This is the central difficulty in translating insight into action. Leaders may leave a coaching conversation with greater clarity, yet action unfolds within conditions that exert their own force—relationships, roles, expectations, competing obligations, established habits, and the consequences attached to choosing differently. The old response is rarely sustained by lack of awareness alone. It is often reinforced by what the situation makes familiar, acceptable, advantageous, or costly to resist.

The question is whether the understanding gained through reflection remains available to the leader to act on.

If coaching is to restore personal agency, insight must become authorship: the first-person experience of acting in a way one can recognise as one’s own, undertake deliberately, and answer for.

Insight and authorship are distinct. Insight works with interpretation—what the leader can discern, explain, and reconsider. Authorship concerns participation—whether the leader can enter the situation from a consciously assumed position rather than merely enact what circumstances have already set in motion.

Insight changes what a leader can see. Authorship changes how they participate in what they do.

Leadership is tested when reflection meets the pressures of a real situation. A leader may understand a familiar tendency, recognise its cost, and intend to respond differently. The critical question is whether, when action is required, they can still act from a position they recognise as their own.

Agency at the Point of Action

We often evaluate leadership through the decision made, the behaviour displayed, the result achieved, and the consequences that follow. These measures are necessary, but they do not tell us how action was experienced by the person acting.

Phenomenology brings this first-person dimension into view.

It asks how action appears to the person who is acting: whether they experience themselves as initiating a response, assuming a stance, or merely being carried along by events, expectations, or a familiar way of responding.

Philosopher Tim Bayne uses the term agentive experiences to describe the phenomenal states associated with first-person agency: the experience of oneself as acting rather than merely undergoing an event.

This gives professional coaching a more precise language for a distinction that is often felt but insufficiently examined. The relevant question is not only what a leader decides or does, but how they experience their relationship with that action.

An action may appear deliberate even as it is shaped by anxiety, deference, or habit. The issue is whether the leader could recognise what was shaping the action and assume responsibility for it.

Authorship, in this fuller sense, involves more than initiating an action.

It involves recognising the conditions that shape a response and taking responsibility for the position adopted within conditions that cannot be fully chosen or controlled.

Before Choice Appears

Authorship can become difficult under pressure.

A leader may recognise a tendency to avoid disagreement yet still experience dissent, in the moment, as a threat to relationship or standing. This is not necessarily a failure of insight or intention; the response may already be forming before the underlying interpretation is recognised.

Organisational conditions can exert a similar influence. What a leader perceives as required may be shaped by:

  • formal authority and role obligation;
  • organisational convention and political necessity;
  • anticipated approval or disapproval;
  • constraints that cannot readily be changed.

These conditions do not eliminate agency. Nor is compliance necessarily its opposite. A leader may support a collective decision, fulfil a role obligation, or accept an unavoidable constraint—and still do so from a position consciously assumed as their own.

Agency can narrow before a decision is made—when habit, authority or anticipated consequence has already shaped what the situation means and what can be imagined within it.

This is why insight alone does not ensure authorship at the point of action. The critical question is whether the leader is taking a position they recognise and can answer for, or simply enacting what the situation has already made seem necessary.

What Endures Through Change

A breakthrough may be emotionally powerful, cognitively compelling, and entirely sincere. Yet its significance cannot be measured only by the intensity of what was understood in the coaching conversation or by the repetition of a preferred behaviour.

The more important question is whether, when a leader encounters later and different conditions, they can participate differently in their action. What may endure through change is a changed capacity to meet new complexity. I propose adaptive fluency as the name for this capacity.

Adaptive fluency is the capacity to remain authorial when a situation is unfamiliar, demanding, or consequential: to recognise what is shaping one’s response and to take a position one can recognise and assume as one’s own.

Agility helps a leader adjust. Resilience helps them withstand disruption and recover. Both matter, but neither necessarily establishes authorship. A leader may adapt quickly or remain effective while still responding from anxiety, deference, habit, or anticipated approval.

Adaptive fluency goes further. It concerns not only whether a leader adapts, but how they understand the situation from which they act. It is the capacity to respond deliberately within conditions of influence and constraint, rather than let an established interpretation determine the response.


What endures is not a fixed behaviour, but a more developed capacity to respond anew.

Seen this way, the developmental work of coaching is not to secure a preferred response, but to expand a person’s capacity to meet changing conditions with greater awareness, discernment, and authorship. A transformational approach serves this deeper purpose by developing not just insight or behaviour, but the capacity to author one’s response as complexity increases.

What a Transformational Approach Requires

If the developmental task is adaptive fluency, then a transformational approach must attend not only to what a leader understands in reflection, but also to how they experience themselves when action is required in organisational life.

  • It begins with close attention to experience at the point of action. The inquiry stays with the leader’s account of what happened before moving too quickly to explanation, diagnosis, or advice. Its purpose is to understand how the situation was experienced, what appeared to be required, and when the leader’s sense of authorship was narrowed or sustained.
  • It also requires clarity about constraint and choice. Leadership action always takes place within conditions that cannot be fully chosen or controlled. The work is to distinguish what cannot be changed in the moment from what is being assumed, feared, anticipated, or accepted without examination. Authorship does not require the removal of constraint. It requires that a leader can recognise the position they are taking within it.
  • A transformational approach must also attend to the relationships and organisational conditions in which action takes place. Power, loyalty, status, expectation, psychological safety, and the cost of difference are not background features of leadership. They shape what leaders believe they can say, challenge, refuse, or support. They are therefore part of the inquiry into action itself.

Finally, it returns reflection to actual moments of action. The relevant question is not only whether a leader did what they intended. It is whether they could recognise what was shaping their response while they were acting, and whether they experienced the action as one they could assume as their own.

Concluding Thought

Insight may begin change. It does not complete it.

The deeper developmental question is whether leaders can carry insight into later situations in which authority, relationship, uncertainty, risk, and consequence make an old response feel necessary. Change becomes consequential when a leader can meet such complexity without immediately losing the capacity to recognise and assume a position in their own action.

This is the movement from insight to authorship. It is not freedom from influence or constraint. It is the development of a more fluent capacity to meet what is present, discern what is shaping the response, and act from a position that can be recognised as one’s own.

The next frontier for professional coaching begins there: in developing leaders who can meet complexity, recognise what shapes their response, and author the actions they take.

Questions for Reflection

Place the practical questions here, after the conclusion, rather than embedding them within the conceptual argument:

  • What did I notice immediately before I agreed, withdrew, complied, or changed direction?

  • At what point did the decision stop feeling like mine?

  • What did I assume was required, expected, permitted, or too costly to question?

  • Which aspects of the situation were fixed, and which did I experience as fixed because of fear, habit, loyalty, or anticipated approval?

  • What was present in the relationship or organisational context that made a different response difficult?

  • What position did I take, and could I recognise and assume it as my own?

  • In a similar situation, what might enable me to respond with greater authorship?
